item.title: Coastal buffalo farms at risk of disappearing
item.description:
There are no ownership documents on paper; there is only a tiny ‘mark’ made on a buffalo’s ear. A dairy and meat market worth nearly Tk 55 billion along the coast stands on this age-old practice. But in the digital age of the 21st century, the nearly 200-year-old marking system no longer holds up as proof of ownership. In recent times, administrative harassment and political malpractice have put the traditional coastal buffalo farms in eight districts at risk of disappearing.

Buffalo rearing on coastal islands and in char areas has long been one of the main pillars of the rural economy. Currently, around 600,000 buffaloes are raised on the islands and chars of Barguna, Patuakhali, Barishal, Bhola, Lakshmipur, Noakhali, Feni and Chattogram. Herds of buffaloes roam freely across the extensive grazing lands of newly emerged coastal islands and chars under the ‘bathan’ (farming) system. These buffaloes have no cattle sheds. These indigenous water buffaloes have an extraordinary ability to survive in char areas through day and night, storms and droughts. However, the number of coastal buffaloes and bathan (buffalo farms) is currently declining at an alarming rate due to various adverse circumstances.

An investigation by Prothom Alo has found that coastal buffalo farms are now under threat due to four factors: shrinking grazing lands, activities of the Forest Department, food shortages caused by climate change, and political ulterior motives. Experts in this sector believe that the livestock sector across the country is grappling with various problems due to the impacts of climate change. Agricultural disasters and food shortages resulting from the destruction of grazing lands are among them. However, coastal buffaloes have the ability to survive these impacts. According to experts, the country does not have a distinct, comprehensive and integrated livestock policy. Formulating a timely policy is essential to preserve the coastal buffalo farm tradition.

Recently, a dispute over proving ownership arose involving 284 buffaloes brought to the grazing land of Kalir Char in Sandwip upazila. The local administration demanded ownership documents from those who had brought the buffaloes. Prothom Alo published a report on the matter on 30 July. At the time, the Sandwip livestock office could not explain what government guidelines existed regarding ownership documents. As the buffaloes remained in the administration's custody for nearly two months, they were deprived of their regular food intake and freedom of movement. The incident brought the government's lack of policy on livestock and grazing land management into sharp focus.

Importance of coastal buffalo farms

There are more than 600,000 buffaloes in around 700 farms across eight coastal districts. This information has been confirmed by data provided by the respective district livestock offices. Of these buffaloes, around 300,000 produce milk annually, while more than 150,000 are used for meat production. Every year, owners sell some buffaloes to cover farm expenses and earn cash.

According to the provisional estimate of the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics (BBS), the livestock sector contributed 1.81 per cent to the country's gross domestic product (GDP) at constant prices in the 2024–25 fiscal year. At current prices, the size of this sector is around Tk 910 billion. However, government statistics do not maintain separate figures for coastal buffalo farms. Prothom Alo's investigation found that the buffalo farms along the coast produce milk and meat worth approximately Tk 55 billion annually.

Twelve buffalo farm (bathan) owners and caretakers from three different areas provided Prothom Alo with figures on the sale of buffalo milk and meat. In addition, according to information gathered from milk and meat markets, traders and herders during field visits, around 300,000 of the 600,000 buffaloes in the eight coastal districts produce milk in rotation every year. If each buffalo produces an average of three litres of milk daily and milk is sold for 300 days a year, the annual value of milk sales from buffalo farms in the eight districts stands at approximately Tk 35.10 billion. On the other hand, if each of the 150,000 buffaloes slaughtered annually produces an average of 240 kilograms of bone-in meat, and the average selling price from the farms is Tk 600 per kilogram, the market value of the meat amounts to Tk 21.60 billion. Accordingly, the total annual value of milk and meat products sold from coastal buffalo farms is around Tk 56.70 billion.

Ability to withstand the impacts of climate change

The impacts of climate change have already put Bangladesh's livestock sector at risk. A study published in the journal Veterinary and Animal Science in 2024 stated that the level of heat stress on livestock in different parts of the country was severe to extremely severe between 1995 and 2022.

A study published in the Journal of Food Quality in 2017 found that around 200 hectares of land used for animal feed in Kalapara, Patuakhali, are affected by salinity every year. This increases food shortages and the risk of various livestock diseases. Another study published in the journal Discover Environment in 2025 found that 63.4 per cent of respondents from three coastal areas reported livestock being injured or killed in cyclones, while 63.6 per cent reported the same during floods.

Temperature rises, cyclones, tidal surges, floods, salinity and various other disasters are increasing along the coast due to climate change. In such circumstances, experts believe that rearing indigenous water buffaloes could offer relative advantages because of their ability to move through wetlands, swim for long periods during floods or tidal surges, consume low-quality feed and naturally cool their bodies in water.

Field-level experience shows that their survival rate during cyclones or tidal surges is much higher than that of other livestock, and their ability to recover quickly is also comparatively stronger. However, the absence of policy recognition and planned management is increasing the risks facing this promising sector day by day.

The marking system and the crisis

The ‘marking system’ has been in practice for nearly 200 years to determine buffalo ownership on coastal chars. Buffalo farm owners cut specific marks on both ears of their buffaloes using knives or blades to distinguish them from others on grazing lands. These are known as their individual ‘marks’. By looking at these marks among large herds, farm owners and herders can easily identify their own buffaloes. However, this system has no legal basis. Although owners can distinguish their buffaloes, the marks are not accepted as proof of ownership when legal complications arise.

On 24 April 2013, the Assistant Judge Court in Companiganj, Noakhali, ordered five buffaloes to be auctioned, refusing to accept the marking system. The buffaloes, which were in the custody of the administration, had drifted from the buffalo farm at Jahajjar Char to the coast of Companiganj. The administration then demanded proof of ownership. Buffalo owner Shahadat Chowdhury told Prothom Alo, “Companiganj police station demanded a large sum of money to release the buffaloes. I sent the bribe to the court. The court ordered the buffaloes to be auctioned and the money deposited in the government treasury. Although I got the buffaloes back after appealing to the High Court, I lost an amount equivalent to the value of the buffaloes.”

Shakila Faruque, livestock expert and acting director general of the Bangladesh Livestock Research Institute, believes that although buffaloes can be identified by their marks, this is not sufficient to prove ownership. It will be difficult to protect bathan (buffalo farms) in the future without digital registration.

Wherever there is grass, there are buffaloes

There is no separate policy to protect grazing lands under Bangladesh's land management system. There is also no clear classification of ‘grazing land’ in the lists of agricultural or government-owned land.

According to herders, food shortages for buffaloes, scarcity of fresh water and security concerns make it essential for them to change grazing lands. A buffalo farm generally has 50 to 500 or more buffaloes. To keep these buffaloes alive, they have to be moved to coastal areas wherever grass is available. However, whenever a herd of buffaloes arrives from one char to another, it creates a stir. Sometimes they face obstruction from local political leaders, sometimes rumours, and at other times administrative complications.

A 2019 study by the Department of Livestock Services stated that the risks of ‘Anthrax, Foot and Mouth Disease’ and ‘Brucellosis’ among livestock in the country's coastal areas are increasing. If guidelines for obtaining permission to relocate grazing lands were in place, administrative complications driven by political motives could be eliminated, while the spread of diseases could also be prevented through health checks of the buffaloes.

Ecosystem centred on buffalo farms

Buffaloes are not just a source of meat or milk; they also play a role in changing the characteristics of newly formed soil, locally known as ‘poysty’ land, on coastal chars. When new grass grows on a char, the movement of buffaloes naturally trims the grass, helping to increase the fertility of the topsoil. Most importantly, there is buffalo dung. The amount of organic fertiliser deposited on char soil every day by thousands of buffaloes accelerates the process of transforming saline char soil into cultivable alluvial soil.

In addition, a small ecosystem develops on the chars around buffalo farms. Various migratory birds, including egrets and mynas, come to feed on insects on the buffaloes' bodies. Small plants and insects that grow in the muddy areas dug up by buffaloes enrich the biodiversity of the chars. Experts believe that if the bathan (buffalo farm) system disappears, the natural soil formation process in char areas will be disrupted, and many rare species of animals and birds will lose their habitats.

Risks increasing, buffalo numbers declining

Livestock offices in five of the eight coastal districts have reported evidence of a decline in buffalo numbers over the past few years. However, herders claim that the number of buffaloes along the coast is declining at an alarming rate.

According to herders there, there were around 25,000 buffaloes in the farms of Jahajjar Char 15 years ago. The number has now fallen to 10,000. The Barishal district livestock officer has said that the number of buffaloes is declining noticeably compared to the past.

Prothom Alo's investigation found that a four-pronged pressure has now emerged behind the contraction of buffalo farms. Many are winding up their farms due to shrinking grazing lands, cases filed by the Forest Department, buffaloes being swept away by cyclones and tidal surges, and administrative harassment. In Subarnachar and Companiganj areas of Noakhali, 10 families each had between 500 and 1,000 buffaloes. Now, only one family in Companiganj has 800 to 900 buffaloes. In Subarnachar, some families now have only 20 to 25 buffaloes each.

Ashraf Uddin, a buffalo farm owner at Dobachar near Sandwip, said, “If my buffaloes are detained somewhere, the government must decide what documents I will have to show.”

Another owner named Nizam Uddin said, “We work ourselves to the point of exhaustion. Due to a lack of space, we hire bulkhead vessels and move the buffaloes from one char to another. If they enter a plantation, the Forest Department files a case. If we move from one char to another, they say the buffaloes are stolen. I cannot do it anymore. I will sell all the buffaloes.”

It is a common occurrence for herds of buffaloes to be swept away from one char to another or from one district to another during cyclones, tidal surges and unusually high tides. Prothom Alo's investigation found that political criminals take advantage of such incidents to seize the buffaloes that drift ashore. As a remedy, buffalo farm owners seek help from the relevant police stations. Taking advantage of the situation, the police offer to settle the matter in exchange for a large sum of money to recover the buffaloes. Otherwise, if the matter is sent to court, complications arise in proving ownership.

Owners have no other proof except the marks they themselves make on the bodies of their buffaloes according to their own preferences. As a result, they face court orders to auction the buffaloes and deposit the money in the government treasury. Helpless buffalo owners are then forced to accept settlement offers in exchange for money. In this way, the cycle of political and administrative power is swallowing up the buffalo farm system.

Existing livestock framework

Various laws and regulations have been formulated at different times, including the Animal Disease Act of 2005 on farm registration, the Animal Disease Prevention Rules of 2008, the National Livestock Extension Policy of 2013, the Animal Slaughter and Meat Quality Control Rules of 2021, and the Bangladesh Livestock Award Policy of 2022. Under the Bangladesh Labour Act of 2006, workers employed at institutions under the Department of Livestock Services are also entitled to appropriate medical treatment and financial benefits if they are injured or suffer losses. However, a comprehensive and independent livestock policy is still absent.

These laws and regulations do not contain any separate policy for coastal buffalo farms, grazing land ownership or char areas endangered by the impacts of climate change. The National Agriculture Policy 2013 also mentions the livestock sector only as an important sub-sector. As a result, the management of buffalo farms and grazing lands largely depends on the old practices developed by buffalo farm owners and herders, known as bathani.

Prothom Alo's investigation found that although there are livestock offices in every upazila, there is no separate monitoring cell or registration process for bathans in char areas. There is no monitoring system or database at the field level concerning livestock ownership, health records or relocation. In addition, a lack of coordination among the local administration, land offices, Forest Department and Department of Livestock Services is increasing disputes over the ownership of buffalo farms and grazing lands, further endangering future livestock management and coastal buffalo farms.

Why a policy is necessary

To achieve Goal 2 of the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), fairness and a legal framework in livestock management are essential to ensure the supply of safe food and nutrition in Bangladesh. On the other hand, coastal buffalo farms could be a sustainable solution for livestock rearing in the face of climate change impacts such as droughts, excessive rainfall, tidal surges and salinity.

Experts believe that every buffalo farm should be brought under digital mapping and a central database should be created, with the Forest Department, Ministry of Land and Department of Livestock Services working together. The ‘silvopasture’ or forest-grassland model could be followed to ensure the free movement of buffaloes inside plantations established by the Forest Department. This would prevent damage to the forest while also providing food for the buffaloes. Such an integrated initiative could transform this centuries-old practice into a modern and profitable industry.

What the authorities are thinking

Sandwip Upazila Livestock Officer Md Nabil Farabi said there are no officially designated grazing lands in this region. He said buffalo rearing could become easier if grazing lands were designated for buffaloes through inter-ministerial coordination. However, he advised buffalo farm owners to register their farms to avoid complications. The buffalo farm owners, however, claim that the concept of a farm is not compatible with the bathan (buffalo farm) system.

The owners and herders have proposed designating grazing lands, registering buffalo births and ownership online, updating sales and transfer information, updating the names and locations of grazing lands, and introducing an online application system to obtain permission before moving buffaloes from one grazing land to another.

The recently retired director general of the Department of Livestock Services, Md Reazul Haque, told Prothom Alo, “The Ministry of Land owns poysty (newly emerged) land. The Forest Department establishes plantations there. We want these lands to be leased to the livestock department for grazing.” Reazul Haque said online registration of buffaloes and the creation of a database were timely initiatives that could be implemented by the department.

However, Shakila Faruque, acting director general of the Livestock Research Institute, believes that instead of leasing the land, provisions could be made to use it as grazing land through an inter-ministerial agreement, depending on when the trees planted by the Forest Department reach maturity. This would ensure the sustainability of newly emerged land.

Immediate action needed

Bathan owners and herders want designated grazing lands for them. They have demanded the construction of raised shelters, ponds and deep tube wells on designated grazing lands. They have also strongly demanded that the government immediately formulate clear regulations to determine buffalo ownership.

Livestock expert Shakila Faruque believes that buffaloes should have unique identity numbers. If these are attached to their ears immediately after birth, they can be identified. Information about the buffaloes and their owners would be stored online against these identity numbers. As a result, owners would be able to locate their buffaloes even if they were swept away by storms and high tides. It would also be possible to establish which calf belongs to which buffalo.

Regarding grazing lands, Shakila Faruque said, “To sustain the buffalo farm system, attention must be paid to grazing land management. Although new land is emerging, the actual area of grazing land is shrinking due to plantations and cultivation. Separate grazing land and ownership policies must be adopted for coastal char areas.” She stressed the importance of inter-departmental coordination for sustainable grazing land management.

Md Abu Syed, senior fellow at the Bangladesh Centre for Advanced Studies (BCAS) and an expert in coastal risk assessment, said buffalo herds roam on isolated and remote islands and chars. The Department of Livestock Services must reach those places and ensure services. At the same time, its capacity must be increased and logistical support provided. Easier communication with buffalo farm owners and herders would make it easier to assess risks and take measures accordingly.

According to experts, simply releasing buffaloes in char areas will not be enough. Sufficient raised shelters or elevated mounds must be constructed there to ensure disaster preparedness. At least one deep tube well must be installed in every large grazing land so that there is no shortage of fresh water during the dry season. They believe that coastal bathans are not merely part of the economy; they are also an integral part of the livelihoods, nutrition and culture of several hundred thousand people.

item.title: Bank Company Act (amendment): Change also needed in the culture of board governance
item.description:
We often explain the crisis in Bangladesh's banking sector through non-performing loans, capital shortfalls, or liquidity crises. However, deep within these problems lies a more significant issue, which is the weakness in bank management and governance. Drawing from my 37 years of experience in banking both at home and abroad, I can say that the difference between a good bank and a weak bank is not just in capital or profit; a significant difference is made by the board of directors. When the board is responsible, management is held accountable. But when the board is captive to family interests, political influence, or personal business interests, the bank becomes a tool to protect the owner's interests rather than an institution serving depositors.

In this context, I view positively the new draft amendment to the Bank Company Act, 1991. On 22 November, the government finalised the draft amendment. Proposals to reduce the tenure of directors, limit family-based control, and keep political figures out of bank leadership are significant. However, alongside amending the law, changes must be made in the board's culture. Without this, it will be difficult to resolve longstanding discrepancies in the banking sector.

Firstly, the proposal to reduce the maximum continuous tenure of directors from 12 years to 6 years, with a three-year break thereafter, is timely. In 2018, the tenure was increased from 6 years to 9 years, and in 2023 it was made 12 years. This has created the opportunity for the same individual to remain on the board for a long time. Prolonged control by the same individual increases conflicts of interest and personal influence. A bank is not anyone's inherited property. If one cannot make an effective contribution in 6 years, it will not be possible in 12 years either.

Secondly, the proposal to reduce the number of family members on the board from three to two and the number of family-controlled firm's representative directors from two to one is important. Family-centric ownership is a significant issue in Bangladesh's banking sector. In many cases, borrowers and decision-makers for loan approval operate within the same circle of interest, increasing the bank's risk and harming depositors. However, reducing the number of members alone is not enough; indirect control through relatives, business partners, and associated firms must also be curtailed.

Thirdly, the proposal to increase the number of independent directors is also positive. It is suggested that at least 4 out of 20 board members and at least 3 on boards with fewer members be independent directors. This is progress compared to before. However, the question remains how effectively only 4 independent directors on a 20-member board can challenge the decisions of ownership. The initial draft by the interim government suggested a maximum 15-member board with at least half being independent directors; the final draft deviated from this.

In my view, at least one-third of the board members should be independent directors. Bangladesh Bank should have a transparent and merit-based panel for appointing them. Merely appointing individuals favoured by the owners as independent directors will not ensure true independence. They should also be prioritised in leading audit, risk management, and nomination committees.

Fourthly, the initiative to operate banks free from political influence is crucial. The proposal to close the possibility for ministers, state ministers, members of parliament, and local government representatives to be directors, managing directors, or chief executive officers of banks is commendable. If political identity or influence is considered in loan approval, it disrupts banking discipline. Loans then cease to be business decisions and become matters of personal favour. However, along with political titleholders, the pathway for indirect influence through close individuals or business interests must also be closed.

Fifthly, the participation of women in the bank's board needs to be increased. The new draft of the Bank Company Act does not have a specific quota for women. However, a separate government policy published on 22 November suggests considering appointing qualified women to one-third of the positions on the boards of state-owned, government-partnered banks and financial institutions. The participation of qualified female professionals should also be increased in private banks. They should have practical skills in finance, law, technology, and risk management.

Sixth, fit and proper or suitability verification needs to be made more effective. In addition to limiting the opportunities for defaulters, individuals involved in financial crimes, or violators of regulatory rules to become directors, it is necessary to verify relevant experience and professional qualifications. A director's competence cannot be assessed solely based on documents. Directors should receive regular training on banking risks, cyber security, money laundering, climate risks, and artificial intelligence. Mandatory training of at least two to three days a year could be introduced.

The financial situation of the banking sector is also warning us. According to Bangladesh Bank, as of September 2026, non-performing loans stood at Tk 6274.04 billion, which is 33.80 per cent of total loans. At the same time, the provision shortfall was Tk 2183.39 billion. In June, this shortfall was Tk 2223.58 billion. On the other hand, by the end of June, the sector's capital adequacy ratio or CRAR had fallen to a negative 3.80 per cent. Under the Basel-3 framework, the minimum capital adequacy ratio is 10 per cent and 12.50 per cent with the capital conservation buffer. This situation reflects poor loan management and governance failures.

Therefore, the proposal to give Bangladesh Bank the power to relax the 10 per cent shareholding limit for strategic investors is positive. However, the investor's financial capability, governance experience, and long-term commitment must be considered. At the same time, the proposal to enforce loan recovery without the opportunity to reschedule after a director leaves the position should be effective.

Finally, ensuring management's independence is essential. The board will make policy decisions, but the managing director must be given professional independence in daily bank operations. No MD can establish good governance if there's a fear of losing their job for rejecting unethical directives from the owner. Therefore, effective supervision by Bangladesh Bank is necessary for both appointing and removing an MD. The central bank must also have the power to dissolve a board, form a new board, and impose penalties for irregularities.

The ownership of a bank can be private, but its accountability is not solely to the owner. It is linked to the savings of millions of depositors, the investments of entrepreneurs, and the stability of the country's economy.

Hence, bank governance is a significant institutional responsibility. While the law can set the framework for this responsibility, its effective implementation requires an independent board, professional management, and strong regulatory oversight. Changing the law is easy; breaking the age-old interest circle and changing the governance culture of a bank is hard. Yet, this difficult task is what must be undertaken now. Because, changing the law alone will not change a bank, the culture of board governance must also change.

#Mamun Rashid is banker and economic analyst

item.title: Garment workers’ minimum wage rises 36% to Tk17,000
item.description:
The Minimum Wage Board has fixed the minimum monthly wage for workers in Bangladesh’s ready-made garment (RMG) industry at Tk17,000, up 36% from the existing Tk12,500, following several rounds of negotiations between factory owners and workers’ representatives.
The decision was reached early Wednesday after a marathon 12-hour meeting at the Minimum Wage Board office in Dhaka’s Segunbagicha, which began at 2pm on Tuesday and ended around 2am Wednesday.
The six-member board decided on the new minimum wage through a vote after representatives of factory owners and workers failed to reach a consensus.
Babul Akhter, the workers’ representative on the board, said four members voted in favour of Tk17,000, while two supported the workers’ final proposal of Tk18,000.
The board subsequently fixed Tk17,000 as the minimum monthly wage for fourth-grade garment workers, marking an increase of Tk4,500 from the existing wage.
According to board sources, factory owners agreed to Tk17,000 during the prolonged negotiations but were unwilling to raise their offer further.
Workers’ representatives, meanwhile, insisted on a minimum wage of Tk18,000, prompting the board to settle the issue through a vote.
Under the new wage structure, third-grade workers will receive a minimum monthly wage of Tk19,200, second-grade workers Tk20,000 and first-grade workers Tk21,500.
The decision follows weeks of labour unrest across major industrial belts, with workers demanding higher wages amid rising living costs.
Workers’ representatives had initially proposed a minimum monthly wage of Tk32,000 before lowering their demand to Tk22,000 and eventually Tk18,000 during successive rounds of negotiations.
The existing minimum wage of Tk12,500 was announced in November 2023 and came into effect in December that year.
The new wage structure is expected to take effect from December 1, with workers receiving their revised salaries in January, in line with an earlier agreement between representatives of factory owners and workers.

item.title: Inmate surge pushes prisons beyond capacity, putting rights at risk
item.description:
Bangladesh’s prisons are grappling with severe overcrowding, with nearly 117,000 inmates being held in facilities designed to accommodate just over 45,000, putting enormous pressure on accommodation, sanitation, healthcare and daily operations.
The scale of the crisis means that, on average, 259 inmates are sharing space intended for every 100. The overcrowding is depriving many prisoners of adequate rest and exposing them to serious health risks.
The situation is particularly alarming for sick inmates, as prison authorities struggle to provide adequate medical care. An increase in arrests in political cases and the prolonged detention of accused persons awaiting trial have further aggravated the problem.
Overcrowding in the country's 68 prisons has thus become more than an administrative challenge, raising serious concerns over human rights and public health.
According to the Department of Prisons, the country's 68 prisons had a combined capacity of 45,186 inmates as of November 22. However, they were holding 116,956 prisoners as of November 23, exceeding their capacity by 71,770.
Of the total inmates, 4,020 are women, while 2,483 are on death row and 170 enjoy division status, according to prison authorities.
Sources said a recent rise in arrests in political cases had added to the pressure on an already overstretched prison system. With a significant number of those arrested being sent to prison, facilities operating beyond capacity are facing further strain.
The impact is being felt across accommodation, food, healthcare, security and overall prison management.
According to prison authorities, the capacity of a prison is determined by the number of inmates it can accommodate while ensuring adequate sanitation, healthcare and security. When the population exceeds twice that capacity, however, every aspect of prison management comes under additional pressure.
A shortage of living space, inadequate ventilation and unhygienic conditions can adversely affect inmates' physical and mental health.
Healthcare is among the most pressing concerns. Although the country's prisons are designed to accommodate just over 45,000 people, more than 116,000 are currently being held there. Providing medical services to such a large population has become increasingly difficult with limited manpower and existing facilities, prison sources said.
Experts warn that overcrowding increases the risk of infectious diseases spreading among inmates. It also makes regular monitoring and treatment difficult for prisoners suffering from chronic conditions such as heart disease, kidney disease, diabetes and hypertension.
Inadequate rest and poor living conditions can further aggravate the health risks for these inmates.
Medical emergencies at night pose an additional challenge. Conditions such as heart attacks, strokes and acute breathing difficulties require immediate medical attention. But overcrowding, limited healthcare facilities and delays in transferring inmates to hospitals can increase the risk of fatal outcomes.
Those concerned say any possible role of delayed treatment or negligence in deaths inside prisons should be thoroughly investigated.
Human rights activists say prison overcrowding cannot be treated simply as a shortage of space. It directly concerns inmates' fundamental rights, human dignity and the state's responsibility to protect them.
Even those detained on criminal charges or convicted of offences retain the right to necessary medical care, safe accommodation and humane living conditions.
Human rights activist Abu Ahmed Faizul Kabir told Dhaka Tribune that overcrowding was undermining inmates' rights to adequate personal space, proper lighting and ventilation, hygienic conditions, rest and medical care.
"Living in cramped conditions increases the risk of infectious diseases and adversely affects inmates' physical and mental health," he said.
"We must remember that imprisonment means restricting a person's freedom, not stripping them of their human dignity and fundamental rights. The prolonged detention of accused persons awaiting trial and delays in the judicial process are making the situation even more complicated," he added.
Faizul Kabir said building new prisons or expanding the capacity of existing facilities alone would not resolve the crisis. Reducing delays in the judicial process, ensuring bail in bailable cases and introducing effective alternatives to unnecessary imprisonment were equally important.
"Alongside expanding prison capacity and improving facilities, it is essential to ensure bail in bailable cases, expedite trials and strengthen alternatives to unnecessary incarceration. The state must take initiatives to transform prisons into centres of reform and rehabilitation, rather than places of punishment alone," he said.
The growing inmate population has also become a major challenge for prison administration. Authorities are struggling to meet the daily needs of a large number of prisoners with limited infrastructure, manpower and medical facilities.
Maintaining discipline while ensuring inmates' security, healthcare and other essential services has placed additional pressure on the administration.
Inspector General of Prisons Brig Gen Md Anwarul Kabir told Dhaka Tribune that overcrowding was a reality the authorities had to manage.
"This is the reality, and we have to accept it. We are trying to manage the situation temporarily with the support and resources available to us," he said.
Asked about inmate deaths and accountability in such cases, he said the authorities immediately investigated the circumstances surrounding each death to determine whether negligence was involved.
"Whenever an inmate dies, we immediately look into the cause of death and whether there was any negligence or anyone was responsible. If anyone is found responsible, departmental action is taken against them," he said.
Those concerned warn that the situation could deteriorate further unless prison infrastructure, healthcare facilities and manpower are expanded in line with the growing inmate population.
They stress that addressing the crisis requires both judicial and administrative measures to reduce the number of prisoners and sustained investment in improving prison accommodation and healthcare services.

item.title: Child marriage rates return to 2006 levels among adolescent girls
item.description:
Child marriage among adolescent girls in Bangladesh has surged since 2019, wiping out 13 years of progress and pushing the prevalence of marriage among girls aged 15–19 back to levels last recorded in 2006, according to data presented by the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA).
The Bangladesh Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS) 2025 shows that 38.9% of girls aged 15–19 are currently married, up from 32.9% in 2019. The increase of 6 percentage points has reversed the progress recorded over the preceding 13 years, when the rate stood at 39% in 2006.
The findings were presented at a dialogue organised by UNFPA in Dhaka on Tuesday, bringing together senior editors and journalists from newspapers, television channels, online news portals and news agencies to discuss proposed reforms to the Child Marriage Restraint Act (CMRA) 2017 and the media's role in addressing child marriage.
Presenting the findings, Iliza Azy, chief of the Adolescents and Youth Unit at UNFPA Bangladesh, highlighted the reversal in progress, drawing on data from MICS, the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics (BBS) and UNICEF covering 2006–2025.
The data also shows that the proportion of girls aged 15–19 married before 18 increased from 28% in 2019 to 33.9% in 2025. Meanwhile, the proportion married before reaching 15 rose from 7.6% to 9.7% over the same period.
The increase has been widespread, with 51 of the country's 64 districts recording a rise in adolescent marriage rates, 19 of which were statistically significant.
Chandpur recorded the steepest increase in marriages before 18, at 19.8 percentage points, followed by Khulna at 18.9 percentage points.
In 2025, Chapainawabganj had the highest prevalence of girls aged 15–19 married before 18, at 53.5%, followed by Satkhira at 51.3%.
Despite the recent reversal among adolescents, the longer-term figures for women aged 20–24 show some progress. According to MICS 2025, 47.2% of women in this age group were married before 18, down from 64.1% in 2006 and 51.4% in 2019.
However, the survey highlights significant socioeconomic and regional disparities. Child marriage before 18 was recorded among 62.5% of women from the poorest households, compared with 31.5% among those from the wealthiest households.
The prevalence was also higher in rural areas, at 49.4%, than in urban areas, at 42.5%.
A joint UNFPA-UNICEF legal review of the CMRA 2017 and its 2018 Rules identified several gaps that limit legal protection for girls. Although the law criminalises child marriage, it does not automatically invalidate the marriage itself.
The review particularly flagged Section 19, which allows marriage below the legal age under special circumstances with a court order, without specifying a minimum age or providing adequate safeguards. It also identified weaknesses in birth and marriage registration, forged birth certificates, inactive child marriage prevention committees and limited prosecutions.
The joint recommendations include repealing Section 19, setting a uniform minimum marriage age of 18 for both women and men, making child marriages voidable at the request of the child, removing criminal liability for children and extending the complaint-filing period from two to six years.
UNFPA Representative in Bangladesh Catherine Breen Kamkong said a law against child marriage could protect girls only when they were aware of their rights and could access an accountable justice system.
She stressed the importance of accurate media reporting on the law and the lived experiences of girls married as children to help policymakers understand the need for reform and raise public awareness about keeping girls in education.
At the dialogue, media professionals committed to expanding evidence-based and ethical reporting on child marriage and contributing to national efforts to reduce the practice.
The event was organised in partnership with the Embassy of the Kingdom of the Netherlands in Bangladesh, ahead of the inaugural International Day for the Elimination of Child, Early and Forced Marriage on November 27.

item.title: Govt employees face double rent for retaining quarters after transfer
item.description:
Government employees who continue occupying official residences after being transferred outside Dhaka and Chittagong city corporation areas will have to pay double the prescribed rent, the Directorate of Government Accommodation has warned.
In a notice, the directorate asked officials and employees to vacate government quarters within the stipulated period under the Bangladesh Allocation Rules, 1982.
The notice said government employees working in the two city corporation areas are eligible for accommodation allocated by the directorate. However, many fail to inform the directorate after being transferred elsewhere for official reasons, while some continue occupying their quarters beyond the permitted period.
Such practices violate the Bangladesh Allocation Rules, 1982, it said.
Employees authorised to retain government accommodation after being transferred outside the designated areas will be charged double the applicable house rent allowance after the stipulated period, according to the notice.
The directorate said many employees claim they are unaware of the double-rent provision and seek waivers on the grounds that their continued occupancy was authorised. However, it has no authority to waive the additional rent payable to the government under the rules. Similar instructions had been issued previously, it added.
Under Rule 15(2) of the Bangladesh Allocation Rules, 1982, employees allotted government accommodation must vacate it within two months of dismissal, removal from service, expiry of a contractual appointment, resignation, transfer, deputation abroad or retirement.
Rule 15(3) allows the government to extend an employee's occupancy for up to six months in cases of dismissal, removal, resignation, retirement or transfer if retaining the accommodation is essential for their children's education.
Meanwhile, Rule 19(1) stipulates that employees authorised to retain government accommodation must pay rent at twice the rate of their entitled house rent allowance under the national pay scale.
The directorate has urged the concerned authorities to ensure strict compliance with the rules, take necessary action within the stipulated timeframe and inform their subordinate officials and employees accordingly.

item.title: Our tourism sector has a friendliness problem
item.description:
On paper, the launch of a three-month tourism carnival in Cox's Bazar is a welcome initiative.
Featuring cultural performances, adventure activities, food festivals, beach sports, and family entertainment, the event reflects a recognition that tourism must be about experiences rather than merely destinations.
With that said, Bangladesh's tourism challenge has never been a lack of attractions.
From the world's longest natural sea beach to the Sundarbans, tea gardens, archaeological sites, hill tracts, rivers, and rich cultural heritage, Bangladesh has always possessed tourism assets. The problem is that possessing attractions and being a tourist-friendly destination are not the same thing.
What we have failed to recognize is the importance of the visitor experience itself. Tourists, whether domestic or international, need more than events and slogans. They need safety, cleanliness, reliable transportation, clear information, quality accommodation, and confidence that they can enjoy their trip without harassment, fraud, or unnecessary inconvenience.
Sadly, we have never quite been able to provide that.
This is especially important for women travellers and families. A destination cannot truly thrive if visitors constantly have to worry about personal security, overcrowding, poor waste management, or inadequate emergency services.
Tourism flourishes where people feel comfortable, welcomed, and protected. These should not be viewed as ancillary issues but rather as the foundation of any serious tourism strategy.
Bangladesh must move beyond treating tourism as a seasonal activity or a series of promotional events. It should be developed as a major economic sector capable of creating jobs, attracting investment, and improving the country's international image.
However, that will require sustained investment in infrastructure, training for service providers, environmental protection, law enforcement, and visitor-friendly governance.
Bangladesh’s tourism sector has long had the potential. But that will only be possible when we can provide a safe, clean, and welcoming environment.

item.title: The need to confront violence against women
item.description:
Bangladesh has spent decades celebrating gains in girls' education, women's employment, and political representation. Yet behind these achievements lies a grim reality we all-too-often ignore: Violence against women remains one of the country's most pervasive and persistent injustices.
Progress cannot be measured solely by economic indicators when millions of women continue to face violence in their homes, workplaces, educational institutions, and online spaces.
This year's theme,"Speak out. Believe survivors. Demand justice," arrives at a moment when silence remains one of the greatest enablers of abuse.
Too often in our nation, public discussions focus on a survivor's conduct rather than a perpetrator's crime.
Too often, women are advised to be more careful instead of men being told to stop abusing.
Victim-blaming remains deeply embedded in our social fabric, discouraging reporting and shielding perpetrators from accountability. If we are to be taken seriously as a nation that is making progress, such regressive attitudes will simply not do.
The problem extends beyond social attitudes. Impunity remains a stubborn reality. Despite the countless documented cases of rape and domestic violence, that we continue to see such an alarming gap between legal protections and their enforcement is telling of how much work needs to be done on this front.
Bangladesh does not lack laws. What it lacks is consistent implementation, survivor-centred support services, timely investigations, and swift justice. Shelters, legal aid, counselling, and protection mechanisms remain inadequate for many women, especially those who need them most.
A nation with aspirations such as ours cannot tolerate a culture where violence against half its population is normalized and who are consistently questioned and doubted. Speaking out against misogyny, believing those who come forward, and demanding accountability from institutions is the bare minimum we can do.

item.title: 2 die after inhaling toxic gas in Satkhira septic tank
item.description:
Two people died, and two others fell sick after inhaling toxic gas from a septic tank in Kaliganj upazila of Satkhira district on Tuesday.
The deceased were identified as Mahananda Sarkar, 35, son of Sanatan Sarkar, and Md Arafat, 16, son of Moni Par, of Bareya village.
Local people said Mahananda went to the septic tank of one Ashraf to clean it and died on the spot after inhaling toxic gas.
Later, Arafat also went to see Mahananda’s condition and died there.
Meanwhile, Golam Hossain, joint convener of Tarali union unit of Jatiyatabadi Swechchhasebak Dal and another person also fell sick as they went to the septic tank while trying to rescue those trapped inside.
However, local people rescued Golam Hossain and the other person and took them to Satkhira Medical College Hospital, said Enamul Haque, a member of Tarali Union Parishad.

item.title: Supply of winter vegetables, high egg production drive down egg price
item.description:
Prices of eggs have decreased by Tk20-25 per dozen over a month. In Rangpur, farmers were selling brown eggs at between Tk9.40 and Tk10.25 per egg on 6 November, compared to Tk11 a month earlier. The retail price of the same eggs in Dhaka fell to Tk10.8 per egg, down from Tk13.3 per egg a month earlier. Farmers estimate their production cost per egg at about Tk9.5.
Stakeholders say that the supply of winter vegetables usually triggers a fall in demand for eggs. They say that consumers complain about an egg syndicate when egg prices are high. However, when prices are low, it becomes obvious that there is no syndicate.
Aminur Rahman (48), owner of 7,000 layer hens in three sheds in Hasnabad of Rangpur Sadar, left his father’s tobacco business and started with 2,000 birds four years ago. He is currently producing at 92% (92 eggs per 100 hens each day) but he is concerned about falling egg prices with the arrival of early varieties of winter vegetables. "An increased supply of vegetables has pushed down egg prices, from Tk11.80 per egg earlier to Tk9 per egg. Supply of cheap vegetables reduces demand for eggs. I fear that the price will fall further during the peak season of winter vegetables," he told this author.
A Bachelors student of agriculture science, Rokonuzzaman Mugdho (23), son of Mohammad Mukul of Thakuradaho of Gangachara, has assumed responsibility of running a farm with 9,000 hens. His father began with 1,000 layer birds in 2014. "I am surprised that the price has fallen so early. Chickens lay more eggs during the winter, and availability of vegetables normally causes the egg price to fall. The market rate of our eggs has declined by almost Tk2 per piece, and the peak season of vegetables is yet to arrive," he said. His father added: "I don't worry too much about the market, I focus on my own farming and business. Layer is a long-term investment and in the short term it can be frustrating. No one can control the price, other than the market itself."
Khandakar Abu Sayeed, a school teacher and poultry farmer in Poran area of Pirgachha, started layer farming with 1,000 birds in 2011. Some 17,000 of his 20,000 hens are laying eggs now. He mentioned that lower production of vegetables and fish pushes up the demand for eggs during the summer when egg supply is usually low. "In winter, vegetables are abundant, commercial egg production increases by at least 5 per cent, and production of duck eggs by 20% or so," he said, explaining the fall in egg prices.
Abdus Salam (35), a trader at Taraganj Bazar, Rangpur, used to sell 7 or 8 thousand eggs at Tk11 each day only a month ago. Despite the price fall by Tk1.5 per egg in his area, he can’t sell more than 5,000 eggs each day now. "Earnings of working people and low income people have fallen, and during winter they buy vegetables, that's why demand for eggs fell," he argued.
In the business hub of Saidpur in northern district of Nilphamari, Shafiqul Islam (54), owner of a wholesale store, said that the price of eggs fluctuates with demand and supply. "Higher supply of eggs and availability of vegetables prompted a price decline." He added that "some people blame producers and traders for price volatility, without truly understanding the market."
Kazi Zahin Hasan, director at Kazi Farms, observed that vegetables and eggs are substitutes for each other. "When winter vegetables become available, consumers prefer to buy winter vegetables, and buy fewer eggs. So the demand for eggs falls in winter, and the price of eggs also falls," he said. “Earlier this year, in summer, we saw that excessive rain flooded vegetable fields, and reduced the supply of vegetables. That prompted consumers to buy more eggs. The demand for eggs increased, and the price also increased. Many government officers expect the price of eggs to be stable, but this expectation is not realistic. When supply exceeds demand, the price will be low. When demand exceeds supply, the price will be high."

South Africa sweep Bangladesh series 2-0
item.description:
CRICKET-RSA-BAN-TEST

South Africa all-rounder Wiaan Mulder ripped through the Bangladesh line-up with a seven-wicket haul to secure a comprehensive victory by an innings and 219 runs before tea on the third day on Wednesday and take the series 2-0.

Mulder, who scored a century on Tuesday before South Africa declared on 494-7, took his first five-wicket test haul and ended with figures of 7-31 as Bangladesh were bowled out for 184.

The visitors were dismissed for 91 first time roundand the gameended inside three days, consolidating South Africa’s place at the top of the World Test Championship standings.

Bangladesh went into bat under cloudy skies on Wednesday as the hosts declared overnight with a 403-run lead.

The visitors, who lost the first test by nine wickets, showed early resistance as they put on a 58-run opening wicket partnership but lost three wickets for 20 runs and were 109-3 at lunch.

Tanzid Hasan (29) feathered a sweep shot behind for Mulder to take the first wicket and he was quickly followed by Mominul Haque, who lasted five balls without scoring as he gloved a ball down the leg side off Mulder

Opener Mahfijul Islam was LBW to Marco Jansen for 38 after failing to offer a shot.

After lunch, Towhid Hridoy hit a brisk 41 off 33 balls before pushing a shortish delivery from Kagiso Rabada to gully.

Mulder bowled Litton Das for 15 and two overs later had the ball swinging to take out Jakir Ali’s wicket and Shoriful Islam next ball.

Captain Najmul Hossain Shanto scored 34 but got a thin edge off Mulder to the keeper and Taskin Ahmed was the next Mulder victim, clean bowled for 10.

The final wicket fell when Mulder caught Khaled Ahmed on the boundary off Jansen.

item.title: US may impose new tariffs on 16 major trading partners, including Bangladesh
item.description:
US President Donald Trump is set to reignite global trade tensions with new tariffs on major trading partners, sources said, undeterred in his protectionist push by major losses by his Republican Party in US midterm elections.

The Trump administration's announcement, expected imminently, will address what it has argued is excess industrial capacity in 16 major US trading partners, three people with knowledge of the matter said on Tuesday.

They include China, which is poised to rack up a record trade surplus of well over $1 trillion in 2026, though the tariff level is expected to remain within the range agreed under the current truce between Trump and his counterpart Xi Jinping.

The prospect of new US tariffs was a further factor weighing on global stock markets on Wednesday as a tech-led rally continued to run out of steam, with Nasdaq futures down over 2 per cent.

"It is another reminder that while the legal justification for tariffs keeps changing, US protectionism is becoming increasingly difficult to unwind," ING analysts wrote in a note.

On Wednesday, Beijing reiterated its opposition to "trade wars" and once again dismissed the notion of overcapacity, but stopped short of threatening retaliation.

"The so-called 'overcapacity' is a false issue, and China opposes using it as an excuse for political manipulation," foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said.

"Both China and the United States should jointly implement the important consensus reached by their heads of state and maintain the stable development of bilateral economic and trade relations," Guo said.

Tariff wall

Analysts say, however, higher US trade barriers against China and other economies are the direction of travel, even if the Democratic Party — which won majorities in both houses of Congress earlier this month — tried to curb Trump's tariff impulses.

The tariffs have in part contributed to higher prices on consumer goods in the US, a major source of discontent among voters.

"Without the two-thirds majority needed to override a presidential veto, Democrats' ability to dismantle the tariff wall will remain limited," ING analysts said in a note.

"Either way, we don't think the blue wave will mark a return to free trade. The Biden years already showed that tariffs in strategically important sectors enjoy support across political camps."

The US-China truce runs until January 10, but many expect it to be extended — potentially as early as next month when Trump and Xi are set to meet again at a G20 gathering in Miami — given the major impact a re-escalation of tit-for-tat hikes similar to those seen in 2025 would have on both economies.

The agreement caps Trump's second-term tariffs on Chinese goods at 20 per cent, in addition to duties of about 25 per cent imposed during his first term. The US has already imposed a 12.5 per cent anti-forced labor duty on all Chinese imports, leaving only 7.5 per cent to reach the 20 per cent cap.

The US and China also are working to cut tariffs on $30 billion of non-strategic imports from each side.

Tailored rates

One of the people said that the duties would be specifically tailored to each country, with goods from Mexico and Norway unlikely to see any immediate levies.

The White House is expected to honor capped tariff rates that were included in finalized US trade deals with partner countries, this person said. These include duty ceilings of 15 per cent on goods from the EU, Japan and South Korea and 19 per cent for Malaysia.

The US also is expected to honor the 20 per cent cap on Trump's second-term tariffs on goods from China, as long as a trade truce with Beijing is extended. If it expires, the Chinese excess capacity rate would rise to a higher level.

The USTR and the White House did not respond to Reuters queries about the pending announcement.

Replacement tariffs

The trading partners included in the probe are China, India, Japan, South Korea, Mexico, Vietnam, Taiwan, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia, Switzerland, Norway, Singapore, Bangladesh and Cambodia, along with the European Union.

USTR launched the excess capacity probe in March, under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, along with a separate investigation into weak or lax enforcement of anti-forced labour laws in 59 countries and the European Union. Together, the duties are meant to rebuild Trump's global "Liberation Day" tariffs that were struck down by the US Supreme Court in February.

The Trump administration has singled out China as the biggest source of excess industrial capacity, which it says is flooding global markets with steel, aluminum, electric vehicles, appliances, solar products and other goods. China says its exports reflect competitive advantages.

The probe is also partly directed at Chinese investment in Southeast Asian countries, including Vietnam, Indonesia and Cambodia, to manufacture goods for the US market and avoid prior US tariffs.

item.title: 123 elephants die across country in 11 years, most killed by electrocution
item.description:
Over the past 11 years, a total of 123 elephants have died in Bangladesh, most of them from electrocution. The shrinking of elephant habitats and human-wildlife conflict are threatening the very survival of these animals. Everyone must therefore take a more humane approach toward elephant conservation.

Forest officials made the remarks at the closing ceremony of a three-day seminar on raising public awareness about elephant conservation in Juri, Moulvibazar. The seminar was organised by the Juri Range of the Sylhet Forest Division under the Elephant Conservation Project.

The closing ceremony began on Friday at a community centre in the Nayabazar area of Juri upazila. It was chaired by Sylhet Divisional Forest Officer Md Abdur Rahman. Among those who spoke were forest conservator for the central region ASM Zahir Uddin and Md Abul Kalam, divisional forest officer at the Wildlife Management and Nature Conservation Division in Moulvibazar.

At the seminar, Forest Conservator Zahir Uddin said 123 elephants died in Bangladesh between the 2015-16 and 2025-26 fiscal years. The highest number of deaths–21 elephants–was recorded in 2019-20.

Many people install electric fences around their fields to protect crops. Most of the elephants died after being electrocuted by these fences.

The forest official said the government has undertaken a three-year project, running from 2025-2028 to conserve elephants. The project includes measures to protect elephants' natural habitats, ensure safe breeding and food security, identify the causes of human-elephant conflict, stabilise elephant populations and reduce mortality.

Zahir Uddin said there are currently 450 elephants in the Chattogram, Mymensingh and Sylhet regions. Everyone must adopt a humane approach to elephant conservation. Otherwise, protecting these animals will become difficult.

Divisional Forest Officer Abul Kalam of the Wildlife Management and Nature Conservation Division said there were 29 domesticated elephants and three wild elephants in the Moulvibazar region.

The wild elephants roam the Patharia Hill Reserve Forest in Juri and Barlekha and forest areas in India's Assam state. All three are female and one has been ill for some time, he said.

At the seminar, local residents called for an elephant sanctuary to be established in Harargaj Reserve Forest. In response, forest officials said a plan has been drawn up under the Elephant Conservation Project to release a male elephant into Latitila Reserve Forest in Juri to increase breeding. A committee has also been formed for the purpose but it did not approve the plan.

For now, the forest department plans to establish an elephant sanctuary in Cox's Bazar. It will later take necessary steps to establish one in Harargaj Forest, depending on its suitability, officials said.

Representatives of local government, police, fire service, agriculture and forest departments, forest villagers, timber traders, environmental activists and journalists attended the seminar. Certificates were distributed among participants at the end.

item.title: Activities-banned Awami League activist killed in explosion while making crude bombs
item.description:
An activist of the Awami League, whose activities now banned, was killed in an explosion while making a crude bomb, in Shibganj, Chapainawabganj.

The incident occurred today, Wednesday afternoon, in the Chowka area of the Monaksha union in the Upazila. At least four people were injured in the explosion.

The deceased is Md Tomas Uddin (35), son of Md Mortuza, from Lambar Tola village in Bishwanathpur, Upazila.

On his Facebook ID (Md Tomas Uddin), Tomas described himself as a member of the Shibganj Upazila Krishak League and an activist of the Awami League.

His Facebook account contains pictures of him participating in various Awami League programmes.

He was known to be close to Samil Uddin Ahmed, a former member of parliament of the Awami League from Chapainawabganj-1 (Shibganj) constituency.

Officer-in-charge (OC) of Shibganj Police Station, Matiur Rahman, told Prothom Alo that the explosion occurred around 2: 30 PM in the Chowka area of the Upazila while making a crude bomb.

A few individuals were making crude bombs in a quiet place beneath banana plants beside a field in the area.

One person was killed, and three to four people were injured in the explosion. They later fled the scene.

OC Matiur Rahman further stated that the police have inspected the incident site, and an investigation has already commenced.

Authorities are looking into how the incident occurred and who was involved.

The body of the deceased has been recovered and sent to the morgue of the 250-bed district hospital for an autopsy.

item.title: Students spend Tk 355m on answer script re-evaluation
item.description:
Nearly one in four candidates who sat this year's HSC and equivalent examinations were dissatisfied with their results.

As a result, a total of 291,211 candidates applied for re-evaluation, covering 1,087,416 answer scripts.

They had to pay Tk 150 per script, bringing their total expenditure to more than Tk 163.1 million.

Earlier, after the results of this year's SSC and equivalent examinations were published, 1,287,926 applications were submitted for answer script re-evaluation.

SSC candidates paid more than Tk 193.1 million in fees. The combined amount for the two examinations exceeded Tk 355 million.

According to Inter-Education Board Coordination Committee data, the results of 23,145 candidates changed following re-scrutiny and re-evaluation of their HSC answer scripts. Of them, 5,548 candidates who had initially failed passed, while 1,620 others got GPA-5 for the first time.

According to the original results published on 31 October, 646,685 of the 1,240,798 candidates passed, recording a pass rate of 52.12 per cent.

Answer scripts re-evaluated for the first time

Previously, re-scrutiny of answer scripts only involved checking whether marks had been added or deducted incorrectly, or whether marks for any question had been omitted. There was no scope to change marks if an examiner had awarded too few or too many marks for an answer. Re-evaluation of answer scripts was introduced for the first time with this year's SSC examinations.

The change in rules has also led to a significant increase in the number of results revised.

According to a Prothom Alo report, 4,585 candidates who had initially failed in this year's SSC examinations passed after re-evaluation, compared with 2,207 last year. Grades changed for 27,836 candidates.

Under the previous system, such errors in evaluation could not be identified through re-scrutiny.

Students pay for examiners' mistakes

The re-scrutiny fee is Tk 150 per paper. In subjects such as Bangla or English, which have two papers, candidates must apply for both papers even if they suspect an error in only one. Under the boards' rules, re-scrutiny of the answer scripts for a single subject therefore costs Tk 300.

For SSC examinations, candidates have also been charged Tk 150 per paper for both written and practical examination scripts. The fee is non-refundable, meaning candidates do not get their money back even if their results change.

Wide disparities among boards

The Mymensingh board recorded the highest rate of result changes, with 14.14 per cent of applicants seeing their results revised. The Technical Education Board followed at 13.23 per cent, while the Cumilla board recorded 11.17 per cent. The Rajshahi board had the lowest rate, at 2.47 per cent.

The Technical Education Board's figures stand out. Of its 17,440 applicants, 2,224 candidates who had initially failed passed after re-evaluation. They account for 40 per cent of all candidates who moved from fail to pass across the 11 boards.

This means that of the 23,145 candidates whose HSC results changed, the initial evaluation of their answer scripts had been incorrect. Students had to pay to have those mistakes corrected.

Asked about the large number of results changed following re-scrutiny and re-evaluation, SM Hafizur Rahman, professor at the Institute of Education and Research at Dhaka University, told Prothom Alo that the current question format, particularly creative questions, should not lead to major differences in assessment between two examiners.

Such discrepancies, he said, indicate a lack of reliability among examiners. Education boards should therefore give greater importance to training and developing reliable examiners.

item.title: Japan unveils rover prototype for Moon water mission
item.description:
JAPAN-SPACE

Japan's space agency unveiled Wednesday a test model of a rover that will travel to the Moon's south pole in a search for water, which could potentially be used for rocket fuel.

Dubbed LUPEX -- Lunar Polar Exploration -- the mission aims to send a Japanese rover to the Moon in 2028 in collaboration with India, which successfully landed a spacecraft near the lunar south pole last year.

The Moon's polar regions contain areas known as permanent shadows, which never see sunlight, and scientists say it is highly likely that water exists there near the lunar surface.

The LUPEX team hopes the rover will gather data on the quantity and quality of the water, helping to determine if it could one day be used to make space exploration more sustainable.

"We ultimately want to use lunar water for rocket fuel," project manager Takeshi Hoshino told reporters on Wednesday.

On the International Space Station, more than 90 percent of water is recycled. But when rockets fly by burning oxygen and hydrogen, that water produced cannot be recovered for reuse, Hoshino explained.

"That's why a key objective is to produce fuel on the Moon for future missions, whether returning to Earth or heading onward to Mars," he said.

The Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) unveiled the four-legged test model that will form part of the LUPEX rover to reporters in Tokyo.

Scientists have been testing its performance under a variety of conditions, including "climbing slopes using a single leg, continuous driving using two legs, and mobility trials under vacuum conditions", Hoshino said.

The rover is expected to identify potential water sources once it lands and drill into the site to collect samples, according to JAXA.

Last year, Japan and India agreed to jointly pursue the LUPEX mission, with India developing the lander and Japan supplying the rover.

Amid an intensifying space race globally, JAXA landed in 2024 an unmanned probe on the Moon -- albeit at a crooked angle -- making it just the fifth country to achieve what is known as a "soft landing".

But Tokyo-based firm ispace last year failed in its attempt to become the first private firm outside the United States to achieve a controlled arrival on the Moon.

Last month, JAXA successfully launched a spacecraft to one of Mars's moons on a world-first mission to retrieve samples, potentially helping unlock the origins of the Solar System and life on Earth.

item.title: 51st BCS: PSC issues instructions for candidates, including entry to exam halls
item.description:
Candidates appearing in the written (MCQ-type) examination of the 51st special Bangladesh Civil Service (BCS) examination must enter their examination halls at least 30 minutes before the examination begins.

No candidate will be allowed to enter the examination hall after 9:30am.

The Bangladesh Public Service Commission (BPSC) issued the instructions in a notice.

In the notice published on Monday (23 November), the commission said registration numbers on the attendance sheets would be arranged in even and odd sequences to avoid any untoward situations in the examination halls.

In addition, the attendance sheets would be prepared by arranging each registration number through a random selection process on a room-by-room basis.

The BPSC said identifying candidates’ seats and examination rooms through the random selection process would take some time.

Therefore, candidates must enter their examination halls at least 30 minutes before the examination begins to identify their respective seats and rooms.

No candidate will be allowed to enter the examination hall after 9:30am.

This instruction is also mentioned in the candidates’ admit cards and the important instructions regarding examination management.

The written (MCQ-type) examination of the 51st special BCS will be held only at centres in Dhaka from 10:00am to 12:00pm on 11 December (Friday).

Details of examination halls, seating arrangements and other important instructions will be published in due course on the BPSC website and the website of Teletalk Bangladesh Limited.

The BPSC published the circular for the 51st special BCS on 24 September in response to requests from the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare and the Ministry of Public Administration to address the acute shortage of doctors in government hospitals across the country.

A total of 5,000 doctors will be recruited to cadre posts through this BCS. Of them, 4,700 will be appointed as assistant surgeons and 300 as assistant dental surgeons.

A total of 44,635 candidates have submitted final applications to sit for the examination.

The BPSC has requested candidates and all concerned to strictly follow its important examination-related instructions to ensure the smooth conduct of the examination and maintain discipline in the examination halls.
